headline: Fort Trumbull Ebb Turns Cooler: Sub Base Porgies Steady, First Bass Sniffing the River Mouth
subhead: The full moon tide pulled bait tight into the Thames this week — now it's a waiting game for the first real push of fall stripers.
body_markdown:
There's a spot off Fort Trumbull where the ebb current pinches down against the old fort wall and kicks up a rip line you can read from fifty yards out — foam streaks, a little chop against the grain, bait getting squeezed through a funnel it doesn't want to be in. That seam has been alive with peanut bunker and silversides all week, and it's the best read on where this fishery is heading. The bait's tightening. The predators are still catching up.

New London Harbor is sitting at 69.4 degrees, which is about right for the first week of September — still warm enough that the porgy and blackfish crowd at the Sub Base structure hasn't slowed a step, but cool enough that the first serious striper interest is starting to show at the river mouth instead of just scattered follows. The full moon that came through the night of the 6th into the 7th did exactly what a hard tide is supposed to do this time of year — it squeezed the bait schools tighter and got fish moving to find them. We flagged this pattern last week, that the building moon toward full would tighten these bait pockets and set up the first real blitz activity within the coming week, and that's precisely the mechanism working right now in the Thames. The blitz itself hasn't landed yet. The setup has.

Down at the Submarine Base rocks and the rubble piles off the base seawall, porgies have been steady on the bottom in 15 to 20 feet, best worked on the last two hours of the incoming when the current slows enough to hold bottom with a size 4 or 6 hook, half a green crab or a piece of clam on a simple high-low rig with just enough sinker to feel bottom without dragging. Blackfish are mixed in on the same structure, and the ones coming over the rail are mostly in the 14 to 16 inch range, taking green crab fished tight to the rocks on the slower part of the tide — don't expect to load the cooler, but there's enough consistency there to make an evening trip worth the gas.

Snapper blues have taken over the upper river, which is normal for early September and a good sign the bait is stacking. They're thick from the Gold Star Bridge pilings up through the flats above it, chasing silversides in schools you can see nervous-watering the surface on a calm evening. Small Kastmasters, quarter-ounce bucktails, or a bare gold hook with a sliver of squid will all draw strikes — light tackle only, this is a fun fishery, not a meat fishery, and it's a good one to bring a kid along for.

The striper piece is the one everybody's watching closest. Bait is building near the river mouth off Pleasure Beach and out toward Ocean Beach, bunker pods tightening the way they do right before the first real predator show. A handful of fish have been picked off drifting live bunker on a fish-finder rig in 12 to 18 feet just outside the river mouth on the dropping tide, and a few schoolies have come off bucktails worked along the current seam where the river current meets the Sound push near Fort Trumbull. But calling it a bite yet would be overselling it. It's stragglers and scouts right now, not a wave.

That's likely to change fast. The next new moon lands September 10, and coastwide that tide has been the trigger point for the fall's first legitimate blitz behavior — bunker schools tightening from the bay systems on down through Narragansett, predators finally committing instead of just shadowing. The Thames sits right in that same current, and the mechanics here match: bait's already stacking at the mouth, water temp is easing down into the low 70s and headed for the striper sweet spot, and the moon is about to strengthen the flow through the whole river system. If that pattern holds the way it usually does, the window from the 10th through the following few days is where this fishery should turn from promising to productive. Fish the last two hours of the ebb at Fort Trumbull where the current necks down against the fort, and watch the surface for that nervous bait activity that tips off feeding fish underneath.

Worth keeping an eye on too — Fishers Island Sound has been showing early bonito and albie interest as those fish push west along the Connecticut shoreline, and the Thames mouth is close enough to catch spillover if that pattern extends. Nothing confirmed in the river yet, but it's the kind of thing that shows up fast once the water and bait line up, so anyone working the mouth on light tackle should keep a small metal rigged and ready just in case.

For the next few days: work the Sub Base structure on the incoming for porgies and blackfish if you want dependable action, hit the river for snapper blues on calm evenings for something easy and fun, and treat the river mouth striper bite as a scouting mission rather than a sure thing until that new moon tide arrives and the bait really gets squeezed.
